tips.title: One pass, one big value parked
tips.body: After pass 1 the **largest** value is at the end and stays there. After pass 2 the second largest is in place. That is why each pass can stop one position earlier, and it tells you at a glance whether a trace is going right.

tips.title: Compared is not swapped
tips.body: Every neighbouring pair is **compared**; only the ones in the wrong order are **swapped**. A question asking for comparisons wants $n-1$ per pass regardless of the data; one asking for swaps depends entirely on the data.

tips.title: Read the question: which pass?
tips.body: A question asking for the list **after the second pass** is testing whether you traced it. Giving the fully sorted list scores nothing. Write the list at the end of every pass as you go, and the right one is already there.

tips.title: n(n−1)/2 for the worst case
tips.body: The total number of comparisons for a full sort of $n$ items is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$: 10 items gives 45. Quote it for an efficiency question rather than counting passes one by one.

steps.title: Two sorts, and why they are on the paper
steps.body:
AQA names exactly **two** sorting algorithms, and you need both: **bubble sort** and **merge sort**. This topic is bubble sort; merge sort has its own.

A sorting algorithm puts a list into order. That sounds trivial, but the exam is never really asking *can you sort a list*. It asks:

- what does the list look like **after one pass**
- **how many** comparisons or swaps happen
- **why** is one algorithm slower than the other

So learn the mechanism, not the result. Writing the sorted list at the end earns almost nothing on its own.

simple to write, slow on long lists
split until every list has one item, then merge pairs back in order
harder to follow, much faster on long lists

steps.title: How bubble sort works
steps.body:
Bubble sort walks along the list comparing **each pair of neighbours**. If they are the wrong way round it **swaps** them. One walk from start to finish is called a **pass**.

After the first pass the largest value has been carried all the way to the end, which is where the name comes from: big values bubble to the top. Because the end of the list is now correct, the next pass can stop one place earlier.

```
SUBROUTINE bubbleSort(a)
   FOR end ← LEN(a) - 1 TO 1 STEP -1
      swapped ← False
      FOR i ← 0 TO end - 1
         IF a[i] > a[i + 1] THEN
            temp ← a[i]
            a[i] ← a[i + 1]
            a[i + 1] ← temp
            swapped ← True
         ENDIF
      ENDFOR
      IF swapped = False THEN
         RETURN a
      ENDIF
   ENDFOR
   RETURN a
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

The **swapped** flag is what lets the algorithm stop early: if a whole pass makes no swaps, the list is already in order and there is nothing left to do.

steps.title: Comparisons are not swaps
steps.body:
This is where most marks go missing. A **comparison** happens every time two neighbours are checked. A **swap** only happens when they were the wrong way round.

So swaps are always fewer than or equal to comparisons, and for an already sorted list the swaps are zero while the comparisons are not.

For a list of $n$ items, the first pass makes $n - 1$ comparisons, the second $n - 2$, and so on:

$$(n-1) + (n-2) + \ldots + 1 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$

For 6 items that is $\frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$, which is exactly what the table above shows.

steps.title: What one pass actually guarantees
steps.body:
A pass does not sort the list. It guarantees exactly one thing: **the largest value not yet placed reaches its final position**.

That is why the exam so often asks for the list after *one* pass rather than the sorted list. It is testing whether you traced the mechanism or just sorted the numbers in your head.

Two traps to avoid:

- **Do not go back to the start** after a swap. Compare positions 0 and 1, then 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, moving forward only.
- **Do not stop early within a pass.** Even after a swap, keep walking to the end of the pass.

steps.body:

Write the list after every comparison, not just at the end. That habit is what stops the careless errors in the exam.

steps.title: Going deeper: why bubble sort is slow
steps.body:
Spec point 3.1.2 is **efficiency**, and this is where the top marks are.

For $n$ items bubble sort makes about $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons, which grows with $n^2$. Double the list and the work roughly **quadruples**. For 10 items that is 45 comparisons; for 100 items it is 4950.

That is the answer to *why is bubble sort inefficient*: not "it is slow" but **the number of comparisons grows with the square of the list length**, so it becomes impractical on long lists.

What bubble sort has going for it is worth a mark too: it is **simple to write**, it needs **no extra memory** beyond one temporary variable for the swap, and on a list that is already nearly sorted the **swapped flag** lets it finish in very few passes, and in a single pass when the list is already in order.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- AQA names two sorts: **bubble sort** and **merge sort**. Linear and binary are *searches*.
- Bubble sort compares **neighbouring pairs** and swaps those in the wrong order. One walk through is a **pass**.
- Each pass carries the largest remaining value to the end, so the next pass can stop one place earlier.
- A **swapped flag** stops the algorithm when a pass makes no swaps.
- **Comparisons are not swaps**: an already sorted list has comparisons but zero swaps.
- For $n$ items: about $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons, so the work grows with $n^2$.
- On 5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2: 5 passes, 15 comparisons, 8 swaps.

questions.prompt: Explain why bubble sort is not a suitable choice for sorting a list of 10 000 items.
questions.solution: Bubble sort compares every neighbouring pair on every pass, so for n items it makes about n(n−1)/2 comparisons. The work therefore grows with the square of the list length: doubling the list roughly quadruples the comparisons. For 10 000 items that is about 50 million comparisons, which is far too slow to be practical. Merge sort splits the list instead of walking it repeatedly, so it handles long lists far better.

questions.modelAnswer: Bubble sort works by comparing every neighbouring pair on every pass, and it needs almost as many passes as there are items. For a list of $n$ items that comes to about $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons, so the amount of work grows with the **square** of the list length: doubling the list roughly **quadruples** the comparisons. A list of 10 items needs 45 comparisons, but 10 000 items needs close to 50 million, which would take far too long to be useful. **Merge sort** repeatedly splits the list instead of walking it over and over, so the work grows far more slowly and it is the sensible choice at that size.

questions.prompt: A student says: *bubble sort is useless, so there is no reason ever to use it.* Evaluate that statement.
questions.solution: The student is right that bubble sort scales badly. Its comparisons grow with the square of the list length, so it is impractical on long lists: 100 items need 4950 comparisons and 10 000 need about 50 million. But useless is too strong. It is very simple to write, which makes it quick to code and hard to get wrong. It needs no extra memory beyond one temporary variable, while merge sort needs room for the lists it builds. On a short list, or one that is already nearly sorted, the swapped flag lets it finish in very few passes, which can beat merge sort. So it is a poor general choice but a reasonable one for small or nearly sorted data.

questions.modelAnswer: The student has a real point. Bubble sort compares every neighbouring pair on every pass, so for $n$ items it makes about $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons and the work grows with the **square** of the length. A list of 100 items already needs 4950 comparisons, and 10 000 items needs close to 50 million, so as a general-purpose sort it is a poor choice. *Useless* goes too far, though. It is **simple to write**, which makes it fast to code and hard to get wrong, and it needs **no extra memory** beyond a single temporary variable for the swap, where merge sort needs space for the lists it builds up. On a **short list**, or one that is **already nearly sorted**, the swapped flag lets it finish in very few passes, which can beat merge sort outright. So the fair judgement is that bubble sort is a poor choice for large data but a reasonable one for small or nearly sorted lists.

examTechnique.body:
Bubble sort questions are nearly always one of three things: the list after one pass, a count of comparisons or swaps, or an explanation of why it is inefficient. Read which of the three is being asked before you start, because writing the fully sorted list when the question said *one pass* earns nothing.

When you trace, write the list after **every comparison**, not just at the end of the pass. It is slower but it is the only reliable way, and the working is often worth a mark by itself.

For efficiency, quote $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ and say that the work grows with $n^2$. *It is slow* is not an answer; *doubling the list roughly quadruples the comparisons* is.
examinerErrors: Giving the fully sorted list when the question asked for the list after one pass.
Going back to the start of the list after a swap. A pass moves forward only.
Counting a comparison as a swap. Every pair is compared; only those out of order are swapped.
Saying an already sorted list needs no comparisons. It needs a full pass of them to discover it is sorted.
Thinking a swap-free pass always happens. It is needed to stop **early**, but a reversed list is still swapping on its last pass and simply runs out of passes at n − 1.
Explaining inefficiency as *it is slow* without the $n^2$ growth or a number to back it up.
Writing the swap as two assignments with no temporary variable, which destroys the first value.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer traces a pass comparison by comparison and shows the list at each stage, separates comparisons from swaps without being asked, and knows that one pass guarantees only that the largest remaining value is in place. On efficiency it quotes $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, explains growth with $n^2$, and puts a number to it. Asked to evaluate, it gives bubble sort its due — simple, no extra memory, one pass on nearly sorted data — before concluding that merge sort is the better general choice.
